summary:
I did this as read-only research on /Users/qiulinfan/Desktop/aipocket. The checkout is on master at 4c619de, not agent-first. Nothing was built, run or edited, so every per-entity figure below marked "est." is an estimate from the code, not a measurement.

**What has been measured so far** (tests/evidence/swarm/README.md, docs/evidence/swarm.md, docs/status.md:20,39):
- Typed arrays: 3000 entities per tick cost 0.353 ms in release and 10.88 ms in the sanitized debug build.
- JSON commands: one round trip costs about 2.7 µs (16.0 ms for 6000 calls). That means roughly 5900 script commands fill a 16 ms frame.
- Instancing cut render CPU for 3000 cubes from 0.90 ms to 0.35 ms (about 117 ns per draw).
- The `perf` command exists (session.cpp:791-805), but no evidence records per-phase world, state or physics times. Before any of the changes below, add a stress sample that reports `perf` phases (plus tools/scripts/dev/gpu_probe.py) at 1k, 3k, 10k and 30k entities, bodies, particles, text lines and scatter copies, and save the results under tests/evidence/perf.

**The common pattern:** nearly everything is rebuilt from scratch every tick or frame, and lookups go through strings.
- **Rebuilt every time:** the world state hash, transform propagation, bounds, physics bodies, draw lists and uniforms, UI paint and text shaping, poses and the exposed-state copies.
- **Found by string:** std::format keys for change detection, std::map<std::string> caches, linear name and command scans, and JSON text on both sides of every script call.

**The cheapest big wins, roughly in order:**
1. Agent-facing runs (MCP tools, run, scenario and bench) default to the -O0 ASan/UBSan build. The swarm evidence shows that build is 25 to 37 times slower than release.
2. The whole world is hashed every tick by default.
3. `EventLog::since` scans up to 100k stored events per call, and both the engine and scripts call it every tick.
4. Contacts are converted to JSON every tick even when no script listens.
5. Headless `step` and scenario frames render every tick.
6. Name lookup is a full tree walk.
7. Multi-component flecs `each()` calls build a fresh query each time.

**What raises the ceilings:**
- **Script calls per frame:** a command table and hashed component lookup (est. 2.7 µs to ~2 µs per call), plus persistent pack views.
- **Entities per tick:** propagating transforms and bounds only for what moved, and hashing at a cadence instead of every tick.
- **Draws per frame:** integer sort keys, then persistent GPU object slots, plus compact instance buffers for scatter copies and particles.
- **Bodies, particles and agents:** a raycast broadphase, physics steps that don't allocate per contact, and a spatial grid for the navigation crowd.

Changing the hash algorithm or cadence, or adding warm starting to physics, changes the golden values. Per AGENTS.md those must be updated deliberately, with the reason in the commit. Changing the default build for runs needs a decision record (ADR).

opportunities.title: Run agent-facing sessions on an optimized, unsanitized build
opportunities.evidence: tools/pocket/src/mcp.rs:180,185 (runtime_start builds and launches the "debug" runtime); mcp.rs:316,320,329 (pocket_scenario, pocket_bench, pocket_run_headless hard-code "debug"); tools/pocket/src/main.rs:56,65,78,94,111,182 (run/test/scenario/bench/editor default --config debug); pocket.toml:20-24 (debug = -O0 + ASan/UBSan) vs 26-30 (release -O2). Measured in tests/evidence/swarm/README.md: typed-array path 10.88 ms debug vs 0.353 ms release (31x); JSON path 404.4 vs 16.0 ms (25x); docs/evidence/swarm.md gives 37-45x ratios.
opportunities.impact: Every tick an agent drives through MCP, and every scenario/bench seed (up to 1800 frames each, mcp.rs:316), costs about 25-37x its release cost, measured. Example: 3000 entities over JSON cost 404 ms per tick in debug vs 16 ms in release. This is the single largest throughput lever for agent loops.
opportunities.plan: Add [configs.dev] to pocket.toml: -O2 -g, POCKET_DEBUG asserts kept, no ASan (optionally -fsanitize=undefined -fsanitize-trap=undefined, which is cheap). Point the MCP tools and run/scenario/bench/editor defaults at it. Keep `pocket test` on the sanitized debug build. Record the swarm and `pocket scenario playground --seeds 5` before and after in tests/evidence/perf. Write an ADR, since status.md treats sanitized debug as the standard runtime.

opportunities.title: Stop hashing the whole world every tick by default; make the hash cheap
opportunities.evidence: engine/app/include/pocket/app/runtime.hpp:35 (hash_every_tick = true). engine/app/src/session.cpp:765-774: every tick does s.dump(), world_->hash() and particles_->hash(). engine/world/src/world.cpp:880-908 (World::hash): an unordered_map entry per entity, two std::function tree walks, has() on all 40 component ops per entity (899-903), derived WorldTransform/Bounds hashed too. engine/core/include/pocket/core/hash.hpp:28-35 (FNV-1a, one multiply per byte). particles.cpp:216-231 (a path string per emitter pool, every particle hashed). Scenarios already pass --no-tick-hash (tools/pocket/src/commands.rs:585); run, editor and MCP runtime_start do not.
opportunities.impact: Est. 0.5-1 µs per entity: 40 flecs has() lookups plus ~340 bytes of byte-serial FNV for a swarm cube. That is about 1.5-3 ms of every 16 ms tick at 3000 entities and 5-10 ms at 10k. It is the largest engine-side per-tick cost that grows with entity count.
opportunities.plan: (a) Hash on a cadence (every 30 ticks, as the network peer already does at session.cpp:815) and on demand in state/report/step. Keep per-tick folding behind an opt-in --tick-hash for determinism tests. (b) Rewrite World::hash to walk flecs tables, whose component sets are known per archetype, instead of 40 has() per entity. Skip serialized=false components. Cache the tree-order key map by a structural version. (c) Mix 8 bytes per multiply. This changes the digests, so update the goldens deliberately.

opportunities.title: EventLog::since: jump to the sequence instead of scanning; gate splash_water
opportunities.evidence: engine/world/src/events.cpp:31-40: since() walks the deque from its oldest event; capacity is 100000 (events.hpp:33), while find() already indexes by seq (events.cpp:46-52). session.cpp:879 calls since(before_physics, 256, "water.entered") every tick. Per-tick `events.since(seen)` is the idiom in samples/walker/scripts/main.ts:42, drive:35, arena:36 and sprites/main.tsx:113. Each match deep-copies the Event and its Json (events.cpp:36).
opportunities.impact: Once the log is full of 100k events (about a minute at 30 events per tick), each call walks roughly 10 MB of Events: est. 0.1-0.3 ms per call, 0.3-1 ms per tick for splash_water plus one script poll. The fix makes it O(new events).
opportunities.plan: Start at index since_seq - front().seq + 1 (clamped) and filter only the new tail. Keep last-seq counters per type so splash_water returns at once when no water.entered was emitted after before_physics. Return spans or const references to avoid copying Events.

opportunities.title: Marshal physics contacts only when a script listens, and not as JSON
opportunities.evidence: session.cpp:734-747: whenever any contact exists, each tick builds a Json object per contact (6 keys plus 2 nested vec3 objects) and dispatches it. jsc_host.cpp:74-80 dumps it and JSC re-parses it. sdk/runtime/physics.ts:54-59 then loops over handlers, which are usually absent because onContacts is opt-in (physics.ts:50-52).
opportunities.impact: Est. about 1 µs per contact (about 14 allocations, a dump, a JSC parse, plus JS objects and GC). A resting pile with 1000 contacts pays about 1 ms per tick for nothing.
opportunities.plan: Have the SDK's first onContacts call turn on contact delivery through a command (for example physics.listen {contacts}), which is also reachable over --serve. Skip the build entirely when nobody listens. When someone listens, share a Float64Array (a, b, normal xyz, point xyz, depth, trigger: 10 doubles per contact) the way world.pack does, and build the objects lazily in the SDK.

opportunities.title: Headless runs and step: render only when someone looks
opportunities.evidence: session.cpp:5383-5395: `step {ticks}` calls frame() once per tick. session.cpp:4280-4288: frame() always calls render_frame(). Every frame records 4 shadow cascades (renderer.cpp:8206-8240), local-light faces (8441-8473), the id pass (8539-8544) and the main pass (8589). Scenario and run_headless launches (commands.rs:585-586, mcp.rs:325-329) render every one of up to 1800 frames. device.cpp:452-460 lets 3 frames be in flight, so GPU time stalls the CPU too.
opportunities.impact: Measured render CPU is 0.35 ms per frame for 3000 cubes, plus GPU work. Rendering only at observation points makes a 600-tick step pay for 1 render instead of 600: est. 1.5-3x more simulated ticks per second for agent loops and scenario sweeps, more in draw-heavy scenes.
opportunities.plan: Make step render once, after its last tick. Add `--render every|last|N` for headless --frames runs, with scenario and bench defaulting to last. Mark the frame stale and render lazily before commands that read pixels or ids (capture, render.pick/ids/visible/compare/views). Keep the per-tick "frame" dispatch.

opportunities.title: Index entity names so World::find is not a full tree walk
opportunities.evidence: world.cpp:311-331: the path is rebuilt one character at a time, and a bare name that is not at the root falls back to walking the whole tree, constructing name(x) as a std::string for every entity. resolve_entity sends every string reference there (session.cpp:4325-4331). Name references are the documented style (AGENTS.md: "Entities are ids, names or paths"). Timelines resolve their tracks by name every tick (timeline.cpp:237). The playground calls world.find each tick and in an expose (samples/playground/scripts/main.ts:46,133).
opportunities.impact: O(entities) per name reference: est. 50-100 µs per call at 3000 entities, so 10 name-based calls cost 0.5-1 ms per tick. An index makes it O(1).
opportunities.plan: Keep an unordered_map<string, small vector of ids> in World::Impl, updated by spawn, rename, reparent, destroy, load and clear. Resolve the first match in tree order with a structural version stamp. Look up paths with flecs lookup on a string_view joined once.

opportunities.title: Cache the flecs queries that per-frame code builds on every call
opportunities.evidence: third_party/flecs/include/flecs.h:35697-35714: world::each() with an entity plus components constructs world.query<Args...>() on every call. Such calls on hot paths include renderer.cpp (13 calls, e.g. 7249, 7257, 7346, 7389, 7480, 7579, 7794, 7943, 8016), session.cpp (update_terrains 901, update_scatters 994, tick_audio 3933), physics.cpp (12 calls, including gather 916, raycast 2372 and each_scattered 840, which means two per ray), animation.cpp (5) and nav.cpp (3). Only World::Impl caches its queries (world.cpp:161-182).
opportunities.impact: Est. 1-5 µs per query creation plus uncached table matching. With 40+ per frame that is about 0.05-0.2 ms per frame, plus 2 per physics raycast, which means per colliding particle per tick. Cached queries also iterate faster.
opportunities.plan: Hold flecs::query members, built once, in Renderer::Impl, Physics::Impl, Session, Animation and Nav for every loop that runs per tick or per frame. Leave one-off scans in rarely used commands (lint, describe) as they are.

opportunities.title: Persistent pack views for the typed-array path
opportunities.evidence: world.cpp:631-655: field_sizes creates, sets and destructs a probe flecs entity on every pack and every unpack, a structural change each time. pack walks the whole tree through a std::function visit and globs each name (world.cpp:678-693; swarm passes name "b*" at samples/swarm/scripts/main.ts:34). Each field of each entity is resolved by a chain of string compares (components.gen.cpp:405-421). Data goes into a temporary vector, then is copied into the shared buffer (session.cpp:4826-4844).
opportunities.impact: Measured 0.353 ms per tick for 3000 entities, about 117 ns per entity. With cached offsets and a cached match list, est. 15-30 ns per entity, so 20k+ entities per tick fit in under 0.5 ms. Typed arrays are the documented scale path (docs/design/world-model.md:68).
opportunities.plan: Cache (component, fields) to byte offsets and sizes, computed once from a default-constructed component with no probe entity. Cache the matched id list keyed by a world structural version, bumped on spawn, destroy, reparent, rename and component add/remove. Write straight into the shared buffer. Unpack through the same offsets, marking modified per table.

opportunities.title: One command table instead of a per-call help search, parameter parse and string chains
opportunities.evidence: session.cpp:5197: command_help is a linear scan over 204 entries (command_help.cpp:235-238). session.cpp:5204 re-parses that command's parameter text into a new vector<string> on every call (command_help.cpp:240-256). Dispatch then runs about 30 starts_with/== tests (session.cpp:5220-5321) and an op chain (world_command at 4593+). world.get and world.set resolve the component through find_ops' linear scan of 40 names up to 3 times (world.cpp:61-66, 401, 409, 418). The JS bridge goes through JSON text both ways (jsc_host.cpp:62-100, 107-120), and each tick also builds a JSON input snapshot (input_map.cpp:158-169).
opportunities.impact: Measured 2.7 µs per JSON round trip, so about 5900 script commands fill a 16 ms frame. Est. 0.4-0.6 µs of that is lookup and parameter work. With a table and hashed component lookup, est. about 2.0 µs per call (about 35% more calls per frame). A typed fast path for get/set could approach about 1 µs.
opportunities.plan: Build once a hash map from name to {help, parsed key set, handler function}. Validate keys against a small sorted array and call the handler directly. Map component names to their ops through a hash map. In jsc_host, keep a protected reference to __pocket_dispatch. The command names and the HTTP surface stay the same, so AGENTS.md's "everything is a command" rule still holds.

opportunities.title: Physics queries: a broadphase structure, no per-ray strings, allocation-free misses
opportunities.evidence: physics.cpp:2366-2437: raycast visits every RigidBody+Collider through a freshly built query, and every scattered capsule (each_scattered, 837-861), on every ray. Mesh colliders build a 12-number std::format key per ray (897) and heap-allocate the BVH stack (2389). placed() allocates a vector for every static child body (20-27). A miss returns fail("no_hit", formatted message) (2437). Per-tick callers: one ray per colliding particle (session.cpp:452-457, particles.cpp:91), occlusion per voice (session.cpp:3896), each camera rig (1294) and vehicle wheels.
opportunities.impact: Cost is O(rays × colliders) with an est. 2-10 µs fixed cost per ray. Example: 500 colliding particles against 200 colliders is est. 3-8 ms per tick. A per-step BVH or grid with cached shapes brings it to O(rays × log colliders), est. under 0.5 ms.
opportunities.plan: Build a static-body BVH or uniform grid in gather and rebuild it only when a static body changes (version counter); keep a small dynamic list beside it. Walk it with a fixed-size stack. Key mesh shapes by entity plus a Transform/Collider change check instead of std::format. Give engine callers an internal raycast that returns std::optional<RayHit>. Cache placed() results per step.

opportunities.title: Move only what moved: dirty transform propagation and bounds
opportunities.evidence: world.cpp:873-876: World::tick propagates from every root and recomputes all bounds every tick. propagate (197-215) does 3 try_get per entity and allocates a children vector per parent (186-195). update_bounds (764-806) does a std::map<EntityId,string> lookup (770), string compares and a std::map<string,…> lookup (774), Mat4::trs and 8 corner transforms per MeshRenderer per tick. idle_frame runs update_transforms twice per frame (session.cpp:1885, 1888).
opportunities.impact: Est. about 0.2 µs per drawn entity per tick: 0.6 ms at 3000, and 2 ms for a 10k-prop level that never moves. With dirty tracking, static scenery costs nothing and the cost scales with moving entities only.
opportunities.plan: Mark moved entities with a Moved tag or flecs per-table change detection, set by world.set, unpack, physics write_back and the motion system. Propagate only the subtrees under moved entities. Cache each MeshRenderer's resolved local AABB and re-resolve only when the mesh string changes. Iterate flecs ordered children without copying them into a vector.

opportunities.title: UI: cache shaped text, repaint only on change, lay out once per frame
opportunities.evidence: painter.cpp:440 calls Font::shape for every visible text line every frame. font.cpp:296-368 runs HarfBuzz and bidi_runs, copies the text and allocates vectors on each call. measure() builds a key string per call (font.cpp:374-381). Glyphs are looked up in a std::map per glyph (font.cpp:66, 248-252). Document nodes live in std::map<NodeId, Node> (document.cpp:254). Layout runs in poll_input and again in render_frame (session.cpp:1784, 1698), and render_frame repaints whenever node_count > 1 (1695-1704).
opportunities.impact: Est. 2-5 µs per shaped line. An editor showing about 300 lines spends roughly 1 ms or more per frame reshaping unchanged text, then rebuilds and uploads the vertex buffers. With a shape cache and retained painting, an idle frame costs close to nothing.
opportunities.plan: Store shaped glyph runs on the Node, invalidated by a change of text, font size, scale or direction, or keep an LRU in Font keyed by (text, px, dir). Add a document dirty flag (ops, hover or focus change, animation, caret blink) and reuse the last vertex and index buffers when the document is clean. Lay out once per frame unless events changed something. Store glyphs in a flat hash map.

opportunities.title: Renderer: integer sort keys and interned handles instead of strings
opportunities.evidence: Per draw per frame: material_key = tex + "|" + normal + "|" + mr (renderer.cpp:7643); material_for builds a 5-part key and looks it up in a std::map<std::string,…> (6386-6391, map declared at 2820); asset_mesh does a std::map lookup (6715-6716); primitive_index compares strings (6935-6943). Each Draw is about 560 B (ObjectUniforms is 448 B, 170 and 237) and goes into a per-frame vector with no reserve (7546). stable_sort moves whole Draws and compares strings (7901-7909). Every pass filters draws through a std::function per draw (8166-8205; cascades 8234, local faces 8466, ids 8544, main 8583-8589). LOD lists are rebuilt per draw per frame with make_shared and std::format (7570-7616).
opportunities.impact: Measured 0.35 ms for 3000 instanced cubes, about 117 ns per draw. Est. 30-50% less CPU per draw from sorting 64-bit keys plus indices with no strings. At the 65536-object cap (renderer.cpp:171) the current path costs est. 7-8 ms.
opportunities.plan: Intern mesh paths, textures and material groups to uint32 ids cached per entity and recomputed when the MeshRenderer changes. Draw stores ids only. Sort a vector of (uint64 key, uint32 index). Reserve from last frame's count. Build per-pass index lists once (in view, casters per cascade or face) instead of calling a std::function per draw. Memoize LOD lists per (mesh, lods).

opportunities.title: Scatter copies and particles as compact instance streams
opportunities.evidence: renderer.cpp:7787-7849 expands every scatter copy into a full Draw copy each frame (`Draw c = d` at 7816, plus inverse_affine and 448 B of uniforms). A Scatter places up to 20000 copies (session.cpp:1039). renderer.cpp:8033-8104 turns every particle into a SpriteDraw with 448 B of ObjectUniforms and a texture string copy (8094), then stable_sorts all sprites (8099-8104).
opportunities.impact: Est. 0.2-0.3 µs of CPU plus 448 B of upload per copy or particle per frame: 20k grass copies cost about 4-6 ms and 9 MB per frame. A compact 48-64 B instance path is est. 10x cheaper.
opportunities.plan: Upload each scatter's instance matrices once, when it is placed (they change only with its placement), and cull per chunk on the CPU or on the GPU. Particles write position, size, color and uv (32-48 B each) into a per-emitter instance buffer, sorted per emitter only when blending needs it.

opportunities.title: Physics step: persistent bodies and allocation-free contacts
opportunities.evidence: gather rebuilds every Body each step with a std::map sleep-timer lookup and std::set inserts (physics.cpp:914-956); the map is cleared and rebuilt every step (2336-2337). Manifold holds two std::vectors (82-88), and solver states are a vector of vectors. Pair tracking uses a std::set built per step (2288). Each ended contact scans all bodies twice (2314-2329, O(ended × bodies)). write_back sets Transform and Velocity on every non-static body, sleeping ones included (958-976). The broadphase is an x-only sort-and-sweep with a per-step index sort (1478-1487), which goes quadratic for stacks and columns. 10 solver iterations without warm starting (physics.hpp:28, physics.cpp:1811).
opportunities.impact: Est. 20-40% off the physics phase at about 1000 bodies, and much more for piles, where the end-contact scan and the sweep-and-prune column effect dominate.
opportunities.plan: Keep bodies in a persistent sparse-set array indexed by entity, with the sleep timer inside Body. Give Manifold fixed-capacity point arrays (4). Use a flat hash set for pairs and an id-to-index map for the end-contact check. Skip write_back for sleeping or unchanged bodies. Choose the sweep axis by variance, or use a uniform grid. Warm starting comes later: it allows fewer iterations but changes the goldens.

opportunities.title: Navigation crowd without O(n²)
opportunities.evidence: nav.cpp:654-659 drops stale runs by calling any_of over all agents for each run. nav.cpp:839-847: every agent scans every other agent for neighbours, allocating `near` and `candidates` vectors per agent per tick (837, 863). The obstacle map is rebuilt per tick (626-640).
opportunities.impact: 500 agents: 250k neighbour checks plus about 1000 allocations per tick (est. 0.5-1 ms). A grid makes it roughly O(n·k).
opportunities.plan: Bucket agents and obstacles in a uniform grid whose cell size is the avoidance reach. Clean up runs with a sorted id vector and binary search. Reuse scratch vectors across agents and ticks.

opportunities.title: Exposed state: one copy per tick and a compact history
opportunities.evidence: session.cpp:761-764: dispatch("state") runs JSON.stringify and an nlohmann parse every tick, then `last_state_ = s` and `state_history_.push_back(StateSample{tick, s})` deep-copy the result twice, plus s.dump() for the hash (767). The history keeps up to 200000 Json samples (about 55 min at 60 Hz). Exposes often call commands themselves: the playground runs nav.info twice plus a find and a get per tick (samples/playground/scripts/main.ts:124-135).
opportunities.impact: Est. 2-5 µs per tick for 10 exposed values, plus the getters' own command calls. The history can reach hundreds of MB in a long editor session.
opportunities.plan: Move s into the history and make last_state_ refer to the newest sample. Store the history column by column (per key: tick and value arrays, strings interned), which is what build_transcript reads. Skip the dispatch when no active context exposes anything.

opportunities.title: Animation: reuse pose buffers and resolve clips once
opportunities.evidence: animation.cpp:906-914 builds new std::map<EntityId, Pose> and std::map<EntityId, Work> every tick. Each animated entity re-resolves its mesh by path through assets.mesh, a std::map<string> lookup (assets.cpp:1636), and its clips by name every tick (animation.cpp:916, 920, 923, 948, 975). compose fills a fresh Pose of matrix vectors per entity per tick (1044-1049), and poses_ is replaced wholesale (1078).
opportunities.impact: Est. 10-20 allocations per animated character per tick, so 100 characters means 1-2k allocations per tick. Reusing buffers cuts the animation phase by est. 30-50%.
opportunities.plan: Keep poses_ entries and their vectors alive and update them in place. Cache the mesh pointer and clip pointers in per-entity animation state, refreshed only when the mesh path or a clip name changes.

opportunities.title: Small per-frame leftovers
opportunities.evidence: update_terrains and update_scatters detect changes by std::format-ing about 20-30 floats per terrain or scatter, once from run_tick and again from render_frame (session.cpp:728, 1685, 906-911, 1008). Timelines::load stat()s the file for every playing timeline every tick (timeline.cpp:220) and applies tracks through JSON get/set (233-250). cluster_lights recomputes 3456 cluster boxes and uploads 27 KB every frame even with no point lights (renderer.cpp:7103-7118, 7207-7208). drain_microtasks parses and runs "void 0" twice per frame (jsc_host.cpp:261-266; session.cpp:820, 4279). Audio is mixed on the main thread inside render_frame (audio.cpp:733-745 via session.cpp:1684). With --history, the recorder rebuilds a std::map per entity every tick (recorder.cpp:32-44).
opportunities.impact: Each costs est. 10-100 µs per frame, together about 0.2-0.5 ms per frame. Main-thread mixing can underrun once a frame exceeds the 80 ms audio queue. The recorder costs ms per tick at thousands of entities when it is on.
opportunities.plan: Compare component structs (generate operator== in pocket gen), and only when flecs reports a change, instead of formatted keys. Stat timeline files on reload or at most once per second. Cache cluster boxes per projection and skip clustering when there are no lights. Drain microtasks through a cached no-op function call. Mix audio on SDL's stream callback thread. Keep recorder state in flat per-entity hash arrays.

opportunities.title: UI SDK: re-render only the mounts that depend on a change, and reorder in linear time
opportunities.evidence: sdk/runtime/ui.ts:522-534: any signal change bumps one global version (138, 146), which re-runs every mount's render and diff. patchChildren calls indexOf and splice for each moved child (ui.ts:486-489, O(n²) on reorders) and builds a string key per child (455-457).
opportunities.impact: A single counter change re-renders and diffs the whole editor or HUD tree in JS, and long reordered lists cost quadratic time. Est. ms per change for large trees.
opportunities.plan: Track dependencies per mount (signals record which mounts read them) and flush only the dirty ones. Use a keyed diff with a position map (longest increasing subsequence) for moves, and numeric keys where possible.

opportunities.title: Persistent GPU object slots: upload only what changed
opportunities.evidence: Every frame rewrites and uploads 448 B per object (renderer.cpp:7928, 8105-8110), recomputing Mat4::trs, inverse_affine and every PBR field (7579-7787). The object buffer and its staging copy are 448 × 65536 B, about 29 MB each (6078-6079). With TAA or motion blur on, an unordered_map of every model is rebuilt per frame (7911-7926).
opportunities.impact: 1.3 MB of upload per frame at 3000 objects and 29 MB at the cap, with static scenery recomputed every frame. With slots, only moved or edited entities are rewritten, so render CPU scales with changes rather than with scene size.
opportunities.plan: Give each MeshRenderer submesh a stable slot in the object buffer (managed by a free list). Write a slot on spawn and when its dirty bits are set (from the dirty-transform work above). Keep prev_model on the GPU by copying it before a write. Draw lists then reference slots through a small per-instance index indirection.

summary:
Read-only review of engine/renderer/src/renderer.cpp (9,083 lines) at branch master/agent-first, checked against samples/showcase. Nothing was built or run, so every millisecond below is an estimate for an M1/M2-class GPU (about 68-100 GB/s and 2.6-3.6 TFLOPS) and should be confirmed with render.stats.gpu.passes before and after each change.

SHOWCASE FRAME, steady state, no MSAA. The depth prepass is on because of AO, fog, TAA and SSR (renderer.cpp:7259). Full resolution is 921,600 px at 1280x720 and 2,073,600 px at 1920x1080; half resolution is 230,400 / 518,400 px. 17 passes are timed, plus the RHI present blit and two full-frame copies:
(0) pocket.sky compute. It runs every frame because timelines/dusk.json animates the sun's rotation, colour and intensity, and the env key includes them (3925). Work: 512x256 fill, 5 prefilter levels (43,648 texels x 64 taps), and a 1-workgroup spherical-harmonics pass.
(1-4) pocket.shadow x4. Each is a 2048x2048 Depth32Float layer, cleared and stored every frame (6092-6100, 8209-8245), with cull mode None (6036).
(5) pocket.shadow.local. A 4096x4096 Depth32Float atlas (7060-7068), fully cleared and stored. It holds up to 43 of its 64 faces of 512x512: the point light (6), the spot (1), and 6 shadowed lanterns x 6 (scene.json:680-1779). Point-light faces are culled only by the light's range sphere (8466-8469).
(6) pocket.ids at full resolution. 4 colour targets (R32Uint, RG16Float, RGBA16Float, RGBA8 = 20 B) plus Depth32Float = 24 B/px, which is 22 MB at 720p and 50 MB at 1080p. Every fragment runs fs_id: 3 texture samples, normal mapping, the decal loop, and a discard (1090-1111).
(7-8) AO and AO blur at half resolution, RG8 (5464, 5535-5568).
(9) pocket.scene at full resolution, RGBA16Float. It clears its own Depth24Plus (8152-8159). The sky is drawn full-screen with depth compare Always (5763-5765, 8577), then every in-view mesh is drawn again with the full shade() (885-1036) and depth Less (5597-5600).
(10) pocket.ssr at full resolution: 48 steps plus 5 bisection steps, each doing a depth load and an inverse-matrix multiply (1268-1327). It writes a scratch target that is copied back (4861).
(11) pocket.taa at full resolution, written to the history target and copied back (5290-5297).
(12) pocket.volume at half resolution, 40 steps (scene.json:80): 20.7M ray steps at 1080p, 9.2M at 720p (1438-1480). It runs after TAA (8717 vs 8741).
(13-16) Bloom: bright, across and down at half resolution, then an add pass that loads and stores the full-resolution HDR target (3319-3322).
(17) pocket.post at full resolution: per pixel, the volumetric upsample does 5 depth loads and 5 inverse-matrix multiplies (1801-1830), then AgX tone mapping.
Then the RHI present blit (engine/rhi/src/device.cpp:430-438).

GEOMETRY: each in-view mesh is submitted in 2 camera passes, plus the cascades whose square it touches, plus every local-light face whose range it reaches. All of them recompute motion vectors in the vertex shader (595-611).

WHAT A FRAME MOVES REGARDLESS OF SCREEN SIZE: 134 MB of shadow depth cleared and stored (67 MB cascades + 67 MB atlas).

AVOIDABLE FULL-SCREEN TRAFFIC: two HDR copy-backs plus the bloom add pass cost 44 MB at 720p and 100 MB at 1080p.

LARGEST STRUCTURAL WASTES:
(a) The scene pass does not reuse the prepass depth. It clears a second depth buffer and shades all opaque overdraw with the most expensive shader.
(b) Both camera pipelines contain a dynamic discard (898, 1100). On Apple GPUs this turns off the hardware's removal of hidden pixels (HSR) for every opaque draw. On desktop GPUs it delays depth writes until after shading. Draws are sorted by texture and mesh, not by distance (7901-7909).
(c) Shadow maps are fully redrawn every frame, even static lights.
(d) SSR, AO, the volumetric upsample, depth of field and motion blur turn the depth buffer back into distance with a 4x4 matrix multiply on every read, instead of reading one shared linear-depth or depth-pyramid (Hi-Z) texture.

Every effect is one uber-shader behind runtime branches. Settings are uniforms and material features are per-object flags. The shaders have no override-constant variants, so the lit shader's register allocation is sized for its most expensive path (16+16-tap soft shadows, anisotropy, sheen, clear coat, a 12-tap frosted-glass blur, 4 terrain layers).

The CPU culls draws against the view frustum, skips casters per cascade square, and uses levels of detail. There is no GPU-driven culling, no Hi-Z, no shadow caching and no texture compression (textures are RGBA8, 6312-6321).

WEB BUILD:
- Every change proposed here except GPU-driven indirect culling and RG11B10 HDR uses core WebGPU only: depth16unorm, override constants, read-only depth attachments, r32float storage textures.
- Limits to respect:
  - The fragment stage already uses 7 of the default 8 storage buffers (bindings 5/8/9/10/13/14 plus objects). Anything new must replace one or request a higher limit.
  - The id pass uses 24 of the 32 bytes allowed per pixel across colour targets (maxColorAttachmentBytesPerSample).
  - indirect-first-instance is optional, and multi-draw indirect is not in core WebGPU.
- On the web the browser runs its own validation and bounds checks and each WebGPU call crosses from WebAssembly to JavaScript, so fewer passes and draws also cut CPU time.

RANKED SAVINGS: first, reuse the prepass depth with an Equal test and pre-test the sky; second, opaque pipelines without discard; third, ping-pong the HDR target and fold bloom into post. These three together are estimated at about 1-3 ms at 720p and 2-6 ms at 1080p for the showcase. After that, in order: shadow-map changes (0.3-1.5 ms, resolution-independent), half-resolution SSR on a Hi-Z pyramid (0.5-1.2 / 1-2.5 ms), and temporal volumetric fog (0.3-0.6 / 0.6-1.2 ms).

opportunities.title: Shadow maps: 16-bit depth, cached local-light faces, clearing only used faces, per-face culling for point lights, staggered far cascades
opportunities.evidence: Cascades are 4 × 2048² Depth32Float (6092-6100), cleared and stored every frame (8209-8245), with cull mode None (6036). The atlas is 4096² Depth32Float (7060-7068), cleared and stored in full every frame (8441-8454) although the showcase uses at most 43 of its 64 faces (point light 6 + spot 1 + 6 shadowed lanterns × 6: scene.json:680-1779, 7039-7047). Each of a point light's 6 faces draws every caster within the light's range sphere, not the face's frustum (8466-8469), so a caster beside a lantern is drawn 6 times instead of 1-3. Per-face culling cuts the vertex work of point-light shadows about 3x. Updating cascades 2-3 every other frame removes about 25-50% of cascade work in scenes with a still sun. Every glossy pixel up to max_roughness 0.6 (renderer.hpp:49) marches 48 steps (renderer.hpp:50) plus 5 bisection steps (1312-1327). A linear-depth texture removes the matrix work (about 10x fewer operations per step). A min-depth Hi-Z pyramid cuts steps from 48+5 to about 10-16. Tracing at half resolution with a bilateral upsample (TAA already smooths the result) cuts rays 4x. Estimated: SSR falls from about 1-2.5 ms to about 0.2-0.4 ms at 1920x1080, and from about 0.5-1.2 ms to 0.1-0.2 ms at 1280x720. The same pyramid is the foundation for GPU occlusion culling (the culling opportunity below) and helps AO. Core WebGPU: r32float can be a storage texture and is read with textureLoad; the mips can be built with render or compute passes.

1. After the id pass, one compute pass writes linear view depth to a full-resolution R32Float and builds a min-depth mip chain (Hi-Z), each level from the one above.
2. Rewrite fs_ssr to take linear depth from the pyramid with the standard Hi-Z traversal, and to trace into a half-resolution RGBA16Float target holding the hit colour and a confidence.

The compute pass adds no storage buffers; the r32float pyramid is a storage texture, so the 8-storage-buffer default is not affected.

opportunities.title: Temporal volumetric fog: per-frame jitter and history so it needs 2-3x fewer steps, later a froxel grid
opportunities.evidence: fs_volume marches 40 steps in the showcase (scene.json:80; clamp 4-128 at 5403) at half resolution (5366) for every pixel, sky included (it marches out to vol.march.y). Each step does an exp, a cascade search, a cascade matrix multiply plus a compare tap (sun_visible 1369-1381), and a cluster lookup with a log plus, per light, a face matrix multiply and compare (local_scatter 1393-1432). The jitter is interleaved gradient noise of the pixel position only (1456), the same every frame. The volume is marched and composited after TAA (8717 vs 8741-8744, composite in fs_post 1881-1884), so TAA never averages its noise away.

A froxel grid (for example 160×90×64 = 921,600 cells, compute-filled and then integrated) makes the cost independent of resolution, about 0.2-0.3 ms. opportunities.title: Smaller per-object rows, uploaded only when they change
opportunities.evidence: ObjectUniforms is 448 B (170, 237-257). It packs the model, the normal matrix and the previous model (3 mat4 = 192 B) with about 15 vec4s of material constants that are the same for every instance of a material. The renderer rewrites every row every frame (7928, 8110). Each draw's sort key is a std::string (7552-7553, sort 7901-7909). Each shadow face and cascade runs a std::function over every draw (8234-8242, 8466-8470).

Hills scale: thousands of scattered copies cost 448 B each every frame (2,000 copies = 0.9 MB per frame, 54 MB/s at 60 fps). On the web that goes through queue.writeBuffer from WebAssembly memory, plus a fragment-stage load of 448 B (objects[in.instance], 886 and 1091) that the browser's robustness transforms add bounds checks to. Splitting into transform rows of about 112 B (two 3x4 matrices plus id and flags) and a material table, with persistent rows for static and scattered instances, cuts uploads more than 4x and CPU time per frame. The GPU gain is small (fewer bytes per vertex and fragment read); the CPU and web gain is larger.
opportunities.plan:
1. Split ObjectUniforms into InstanceRow {model 3x4, prev 3x4, id, flags, material index, joint base, sway} and MaterialRow (pbr, emissive, optics, volume, sheen, spec, aniso, terrain, uv_rect), deduplicated by material key.
2. Compute the normal matrix in the vertex shader from model (inverse-transpose of the 3x3), or store a uniform-scale flag.
3. Keep scattered copies' rows resident in a stable range, rewritten only when World::derived_instances changes.
4. Track dirty ranges and upload only those.
5. Replace the string sort keys with interned integer ids and the std::function keep callbacks with templated lambdas.
Web: MaterialRow needs one more storage buffer. It can take over one of the existing ones (fold sh and probe_sh together), because the fragment stage is at 7 of 8.

opportunities.title: GPU-driven culling with a Hi-Z pyramid and indirect draws, for large scenes
opportunities.evidence: All culling is on the CPU, per draw, against bounding spheres: the camera frustum (7852-7897), cascade squares (8234-8241), light range spheres (8466-8469). Probe captures draw every draw into all 6 faces with no culling at all (8342). There is no occlusion culling, so hidden geometry is still transformed in the id pass, the scene pass, up to 4 cascades and every local face. The docs list hills at 1.15M triangles (docs/design/rendering.md:110) with 2,242 caster draws (rendering.md:27). The draws pass instance_index as firstInstance to address object rows (8203).
opportunities.impact: Only matters in big scenes. In hills-like terrain with heavy occlusion, a compute pass that culls instances against the frustum and the previous frame's Hi-Z, then compacts them into indirect draws, could remove 30-70% of the vertex and shadow work: an estimated 1-3 ms in vertex-bound frames. The showcase (47 meshes) gains nothing. On the web, indirect draws with a non-zero first instance need the optional 'indirect-first-instance' feature, and multi-draw indirect is not in core WebGPU. The portable route is a compacted instance-index buffer read as objects[remap[base + instance_index]], one indirect draw per run.
opportunities.plan:
First, add per-face frustum culling to probe captures, which is small. Then, reusing the Hi-Z pyramid from the SSR opportunity:
1. Upload instance spheres once (from the persistent rows of the per-object-rows opportunity).
2. A compute pass per camera and per cascade tests frustum plus Hi-Z (last frame's pyramid, reprojected) and appends visible instance indices into per-run ranges.
3. Write DrawIndexedIndirect arguments per run.
4. Have the vertex shaders read objects[visible[instance_index + run_base]], with run_base as a dynamic-offset uniform or push-style per-run constant.
5. Fall back to CPU culling when the adapter lacks indirect support, or keep the remap approach everywhere.

opportunities.title: Texture and render-target formats: compressed textures, a thinner surface target, optionally smaller HDR
opportunities.evidence: Every texture is uploaded as RGBA8Unorm with a full mip chain built on the CPU (6312-6321), with no BC, ASTC or ETC2 anywhere in engine/. The terrain layer arrays are 512² × 10 levels (234), the decal arrays 256² × 16 layers (230). The surface target is RGBA16Float (213) for an octahedral normal plus roughness and metallic, all of which fit in 8 bits. HDR, TAA history ×2, fx, glass and water copies, bloom ×2 and volume are all RGBA16Float (61).
opportunities.impact: BC7 or ASTC-4x4 cut texture memory and sampling bandwidth 4x (BC1 8x). This mostly speeds the 3-6 material samples per fragment in textured scenes (glTF assets, terrain layers) and shortens loading and upload, including web download size. A surface target in RGBA8Unorm or RGB10A2Unorm (both core WebGPU) saves 4 B/px on the id-pass write and SSR read: 3.7 MB at 720p and 8.3 MB at 1080p each way. RG11B10Ufloat HDR would halve every HDR touch (about 80 MB per frame at 1080p) but needs the optional 'rg11b10ufloat-renderable' feature on the web and risks banding in TAA history, so treat it as an experiment.
opportunities.plan:
Do the cheap part now: switch kSurfaceFormat (213) to RGBA8Unorm (oct normal ×0.5+0.5, roughness, metallic) or RGB10A2Unorm, and adapt the oct_encode output and the decode in fs_ssr (1286-1290) and in water (1654, 1686).
Texture compression, later:
1. Add BC7/BC5 (desktop, and Chrome on Mac exposes texture-compression-bc) and ASTC (iOS/Android) encoders to `pocket pack` and asset import, using basisu/KTX2 transcoding or offline encoding.
2. Request the texture-compression features when the adapter has them (engine/rhi/src/device.cpp:332-337 currently requests only timestamp-query).
3. Fall back to RGBA8 when they are missing.
Only then try RG11B10 HDR, behind a feature check.

summary:
Read-only reach study of /Users/qiulinfan/Desktop/aipocket (branch now named master). I built nothing and ran nothing. I read AGENTS.md, docs/status.md, docs/positioning.md, all of docs/design/*.md, the SDK (sdk/runtime/*.ts), the 13 samples and the hot paths in engine/.

Size of the engine today: 204 runtime commands (engine/app/src/session.cpp:5486), 40 components plus 9 records (engine/world/meta/components.toml) and about 43k lines of C++. Rendering, terrain, water, audio, localization, UI, Tiled maps and the agent instruments are very deep. Gameplay plumbing and distribution are thin: input, combat, data, structure and platforms.

Coverage by genre:
- **2D platformer:** strong. Body2D handles slopes, one-way tiles, platforms, stacking, bounce and friction; Tiled maps, animated tiles and platformer nav links all work. Gaps: no body-to-body sensors, so pickups are Math.hypot checks (samples/sprites/scripts/main.tsx:77-85). No additive or flash VFX. Sprite clips are grid-only.
- **3D platformer and adventure movement:** good. Character, CameraRig and the walker sample cover it. But no humanoid ever passes through the pipeline: the only skinned asset is a generated two-joint arm (samples/assets/assets/arm.glb, 6,696 bytes).
- **Third-person action and combat:** partial. Present: animation state machines with 1D blend spaces, layers, IK, look-at, root motion, hit-stop (time.scale), camera shake and rumble. Missing: animation events, bone attachments and hitboxes, box or capsule overlaps, ragdolls, crouch and lock-on.
- **First-person:** blocked. There is no cursor lock or pointer lock, mouse buttons cannot be bound to actions, and the renderer uses one camera only, so there is no viewmodel.
- **Top-down and twin-stick:** OK through TopDown2D, rig offset mode and per-player pads. Mouse aim and fire hit the same input gap.
- **RTS and many units:** partial. Strong: NavAgent crowds, formations, queueing, and typed arrays (3000 entities in 0.35 ms). Limits:
  - Agent avoidance is O(n²) (engine/nav/src/nav.cpp:839, 943).
  - Joint matrices are capped at 16384 per frame, about 250 humanoid rigs (engine/renderer/src/renderer.cpp:2480, 7735).
  - No minimap or fog-of-war render target.
- **Racing:** decent. Vehicle and the drive sample work. No splines for tracks or AI lines; tyre model is a friction circle.
- **Puzzle:** good: grids, tweens, UI, scenarios.
- **Narrative:** partial. Localization (plurals, RTL, CJK), timeline events and audio ducking exist. Missing: a dialogue runtime, rich text and font families, and npm packages are refused, so inkjs is unavailable (tools/pocket/src/ts.rs:245).
- **Roguelike and procedural generation:** partial. Present: one seeded random(), runtime tile edits, nav rebake. Missing:
  - noise and separate RNG streams in the SDK
  - creating a tile map (tilemap.create) or a mesh (mesh.create) at runtime
  - tile and terrain edits are not kept in save slots (session.cpp:3486-3496)
- **Multiplayer:** lockstep only, with WebSocket browser peers and rejoin by replay. No rollback, client-server, relay or WebRTC (docs/design/networking.md:58).
- **Mobile:** touch and gestures through the web build only. No native packaging, no virtual controls bound to actions, no touch-action CSS.
- **Web:** strong (4.0 to 7.1 MB runtime, IndexedDB saves). WebGPU only; no pointer lock or fullscreen.
- **Desktop shipping:** macOS only and unsigned. No Windows or Linux (pocket.toml:82; engine/platform/src/platform.cpp:244).
- **Saves:** slots work, but world edits are not saved.
- **Accessibility:** UI keyboard and pad navigation plus text snapshots only. AccessKit is deferred (docs/decisions/0004-ui-architecture.md:29); no captions, no text scale.
- **Localization and audio:** strong.

Authoring workflow:
- **Blender and Tiled:** strong (headless conversion, components from custom properties, live relink).
- **Gameplay data cannot ride on Blender or Tiled properties:** a project cannot declare its own components, so the engine skips those properties (AGENTS.md:77, docs/design/assets.md:58).
- **Clips must sit in the mesh's own file** (engine/renderer/src/animation.cpp:920). Mixamo-style animation packs do not work.
- **Editor camera:** it orbits the world origin and moves the game's own camera (editor/orbit.ts:19). It cannot pan or focus on the selection, and the editor has no prefab palette.
- **Feel tuning:** there are no tunable values that a director can edit in the inspector.

Highest value for effort:
1. Cursor lock and mouse buttons as actions.
2. Gameplay components declared by the project.
3. A combat kit: animation events, attachments to bones, more physics query shapes.
4. npm imports plus a seeded Math.random.
5. A 2D kit: sensors, additive blending, Aseprite sheets.

The largest single gain is Windows and Linux builds, at large effort.

opportunities.title: Cursor lock and mouse buttons as input actions (unblocks first-person and mouse look)
opportunities.evidence: engine/platform/src/platform.cpp:278-282 reads the mouse's relative motion (xrel), but nothing in engine/ ever turns on SDL's relative mouse mode, so the cursor stops at the window edge and mouse:x stops changing. engine/app/src/input_map.cpp:91-111: apply() handles key, pad, mouse-move and wheel events, and the default case (line 111) drops mouse button presses, so 'fire = mouse:left' cannot be bound. docs/design/input.md:15 lists only keys, pad, mouse axes and wheel as bindings. tools/pocket/src/web_shell.html:5,11 has only a viewport meta tag: no requestPointerLock, fullscreen or touch-action.
opportunities.impact: Turns first-person from blocked into feasible. Makes mouse-orbit third-person cameras usable (a CameraRig orbit_x bound to mouse:x dies at the window edge). Gives twin-stick, RTS and click-to-move games mouse buttons through the same action maps that scenarios, agents and the lockstep network already drive. Web keyboard-and-mouse games get pointer lock.
opportunities.plan: 1) Platform: add set_cursor({locked, visible}), which calls SDL_SetWindowRelativeMouseMode and SDL_HideCursor; SDL3's Emscripten port turns relative mode into Pointer Lock, and the web shell requests it on the canvas's first click. 2) Add an input.cursor {locked?, visible?} command and SDK input.lockCursor(), an `[input] cursor` key in project.toml, and Escape to release it. It is journaled, does nothing headless, and the editor never locks while its scene pane has focus. 3) InputMap::apply: add MouseDown and MouseUp cases with sources mouse:left, mouse:right, mouse:middle, mouse:x1 and mouse:x2; input.press and input.hold accept them, and the editor's Input tab Press captures them. 4) web_shell.html: touch-action:none on the canvas and a pocket.fullscreen() call. 5) Tests: runtime_tests [input][mouse] for a fire action bound to mouse:left; a walker scenario that turns the orbit rig with mouse:x.

opportunities.title: Gameplay components declared by the project (enemy stats, teams, inventory, tunables)
opportunities.evidence: AGENTS.md:77: components are declared only in engine/world/meta/components.toml, which means rebuilding the engine. engine/world/src/world.cpp:47-66: ops_table() is a static vector generated from the component list; find_ops does a linear lookup and get/set return unknown_component (world.cpp:411). Health (components.toml:36) is the only gameplay-data component, and it is hard-coded. docs/design/assets.md:58: Blender custom properties that name no component are skipped with a warning; Tiled 'Component.field' properties (docs/design/tilemaps.md) hit the same wall. Samples keep gameplay state in script Maps and Sets (samples/playground/scripts/main.ts:9, samples/sprites/scripts/main.tsx:11). That state is outside world.query, the state hash, save slots, the recorder and the inspector unless it is hand-exposed.
opportunities.impact: Affects every genre. Level data such as enemy kind, loot table, door/key links, waypoints and dialogue IDs can come from Blender and Tiled. Agents can query and time-travel gameplay state with world.query, recorder.track and events.why. Saves become automatic instead of onSave plumbing. Game-feel tuning becomes inspector sliders on a Tuning entity that a human director edits live. This is the core of the 'grow without collapse' and 'perception, not screenshots' promises in docs/positioning.md.
opportunities.plan: 1) A project-level components.toml in the same schema as engine/world/meta/components.toml; gen.rs already parses it, so `pocket gen` emits project TypeScript types and `pocket check` types world.get(e, "Enemy"). 2) World: turn ops_table into a registry that the session extends at project load with dynamic ComponentOps. Storage is a flecs runtime component per name holding a Json value checked against the schema (defaults, types). Hashing uses canonical JSON. save, load, recorder and schema already iterate the ops, so they pick these up. 3) Blender extras and Tiled properties work automatically because they go through world.set by name. 4) world.pack later, for f32 fields. 5) Evidence: an Enemy {hp, speed, kind} in the playground, set from a Blender property, queried, saved and loaded; runtime_tests [components][project]; the editor's inspector edits it.

opportunities.title: 3D combat kit: animation events, attachments to bones, more query shapes
opportunities.evidence: engine/renderer/src/animation.cpp:412 and :1090 are the only animation events, animation.state and animation.finished; clips have no markers, so there is no hit window, footstep or effect timing. None of the 40 components attaches an entity to a joint: a weapon in a hand, or a hitbox on a forearm, needs animation.pose, which returns the whole skeleton as JSON on every call. engine/physics/src/physics.cpp:20-21: placed() composes parent transforms only for static bodies. The RigidBody doc (components.toml:459-460) says kinematic bodies must be roots, so a kinematic trigger hitbox under a moving character is placed by its local Transform as if it were the world. docs/design/physics.md:90-91 and engine/app/src/command_help.cpp:116,118: overlap and sweep are sphere-only, and raycast returns only the first hit with no way to exclude an entity. docs/design/physics.md:102: no crouch, and characters are never pushed.
opportunities.impact: Third-person action, melee combat, souls-likes, brawlers and shooters can time hits to the animation, put swords, guns, muzzle flashes and hats on bones, hit with box or capsule volumes, and play footstep sounds and effects. Combined with AnimationGraph and IK, this unlocks the genre the positioning names first (third-person adventure).
opportunities.plan: 1) Markers: the Blender conversion script (engine/assets/src/import.cpp:505-540) writes each action's pose_markers into the GLB's animation extras. A sidecar <mesh>.events.json is also accepted. The glTF reader stores them as AnimationClip::markers. In Animation::step, after advancing time (animation.cpp:928-960), emit animation.event {clip, name, time, layer} for every marker crossed in (old, new], including loop wraps and layers, with the entity as subject. Add sprite.event for marked sprite-clip frames. 2) An Attach {target, node, offset, rotation} component, applied after the animation step: the entity's world Transform becomes target world × the joint's global × offset (or just the target's transform without a node). Document the one-tick lag for physics. Let kinematic triggers be parented by composing parents in placed() for any kind, from a per-step cache. 3) physics.overlap {shape: box|capsule, half, rotation, exclude} through the existing overlap_pair (physics.cpp:1118); physics.raycast {exclude, all}. 4) Proof: a sword attached to the arm's tip joint, a swing_open/swing_close marker window, a scenario counting hits; runtime_tests [animevents] [attach] [overlap].

opportunities.title: npm packages in the bundler, and a seeded Math.random
opportunities.evidence: tools/pocket/src/ts.rs:245 rejects every bare import ("only relative paths and pocket/* are supported"). Yet the bundle is already a CommonJS-style registry (ts.rs:1-7), so CommonJS modules would fit without a transform. Nothing in sdk/runtime or engine/script overrides Math.random or Date.now (grep finds none). AGENTS.md says randomness must come from the seeded random(), and docs/design/networking.md:50 notes that scripts using Math functions drift across engines. Models write Math.random() by habit.
opportunities.impact: Opens the JavaScript ecosystem that every model knows: inkjs and yarn for dialogue (narrative), rot.js for dungeons, field of view and pathfinding (roguelikes), simplex-noise (procedural generation), behaviour-tree and state-machine libraries (AI). The seeded override keeps replays, scenarios run at many seeds, and lockstep games deterministic even when an agent or a library calls Math.random.
opportunities.plan: 1) ts.rs resolve(): for bare specifiers, walk up to node_modules/<pkg>/package.json and pick exports (import or default), then module, then main. Bundle ES modules through the existing path and wrap CommonJS files as registry functions. Refuse Node built-ins with a clear message. 2) Pass node_modules type roots to `pocket check`. 3) Optionally `pocket add <pkg>`: fetch the registry tarball by sha256 into a lockfile, no Node needed (deps.rs already fetches pinned artifacts). 4) At SDK start (pocket.ts), set Math.random to a seeded stream, with an opt-out; world.lint warns when project code uses Math.random or Date.now. 5) Evidence: a ui-sample dialogue driven by inkjs, plus the agent-eval task 'add a dialogue with two choices'.

opportunities.title: 2D gameplay kit: sensors between bodies, additive and flash sprites, Aseprite sheets
opportunities.evidence: engine/physics/src/tiles.cpp emits only body2d.landed and body2d.bounced; nothing reports two Body2D boxes overlapping. docs/design/tilemaps.md:77 tells scripts to 'check what touches what with distances', and samples/sprites/scripts/main.tsx:77-85 collects coins with Math.hypot and one world.get per coin per tick. Body2D is an axis-aligned box only (components.toml:504). engine/renderer/src/renderer.cpp:5653-5662: sprites and particles share one alpha-blended pipeline, and Sprite.color only multiplies, so there is no additive fire or magic and no white hit-flash. docs/design/sprites.md:30: clips are uniform grid cells at one fps, so Aseprite and TexturePacker sheets (packed rectangles, per-frame durations, tags) cannot be used.
opportunities.impact: Every 2D genre (platformers, top-down shooters, bullet hells, roguelikes, metroidvanias) gets engine-side pickups, hazards and projectile hits with events agents can trace (events.why), standard 2D effects and game feel, and the most common pixel-art tool's exports.
opportunities.plan: 1) Body2D.sensor plus layer and mask (or an Area2D {size, offset} component). In tiles.cpp, after resolving bodies against each other, sweep and prune AABB pairs on x and emit body2d.entered and body2d.left with both ids and paths. Add body2d.overlap {rect|point} and body2d.raycast queries. 2) A blend field ('alpha' or 'additive') on Sprite and ParticleEmitter (a second pipeline variant, sorted runs), plus Sprite.flash colour and amount mixed in fs_unlit. 3) sprites.loadSheet('assets/hero.json'): parse Aseprite and TexturePacker JSON into clips with a rectangle and duration per frame; SpriteAnimation frames become rectangles. 4) Move the sprites sample's coins to sensors; runtime_tests [body2d][sensor]; a capture of additive sparks under bloom.

opportunities.title: Gameplay code structure: ids in events, event subscriptions, per-entity behaviours, AI sight queries
opportunities.evidence: engine/physics/src/physics.cpp:2304-2305: collision and trigger events carry only the paths of a and b. samples/walker/scripts/main.ts:42-51 polls events.since every tick and finds the other entity again by string (`world.find(String(e.data.b).replace(/^\//, ""))`). sdk/runtime/events.ts:13-35 has emit, since, recent and why but no subscription. Among the 204 commands there is no perception query (line of sight with a field-of-view cone) and no AI-as-data component comparable to AnimationGraph.
opportunities.impact: Agent-written games stay organized as they grow (positioning job 3, 'grow without collapse'). Enemy, NPC and pickup logic is attached by entity type rather than piled into one onTick. AI decisions can be inspected the way AnimationGraph states are. This helps action, stealth, RTS and adventure games most.

opportunities.title: Editor for level design: its own camera (pan, focus, fly) and a prefab palette
opportunities.evidence: editor/orbit.ts:19 always orbits a target at {0,0,0}, and applyOrbit (orbit.ts:23 onward) writes the scene's own active Camera Transform, so orbiting changes the game camera that Save then stores. editor/main.tsx:1044-1054 handles only yaw, pitch and zoom distance (docs/editor.md:17 says 'drag orbits the camera; wheel zooms'), with no pan, frame-selection or fly mode. The 240-unit drive terrain or a large Blender level cannot be navigated. 'prefab' appears nowhere in editor/main.tsx: prefabs cannot be browsed, placed or edited there, and instances are copies with no link back to the prefab file (docs/design/world-model.md, Scenes and prefabs).
opportunities.impact: Level design in the editor for any 3D genre. Human directors and agents operating the editor through ui.* can lay out enemies, pickups and props from a palette, and the game camera stops being corrupted by looking around.
opportunities.plan: 1) Draw the scene pane from an editor-only view through Renderer::set_view (already used by render.views), not the scene's camera entity. 2) Middle-drag or Shift-drag pans, F frames the selection (from Bounds), right-drag with WASD flies, and the orbit pivot follows the selection; all kept in .pocket/editor.json. 3) A Prefabs tab listing prefabs/*.json with render.views thumbnails; drag or Place instantiates at the ray hit (physics.raycast, as the terrain brush does); 'Apply to prefab' writes world.save_prefab. 4) runtime_tests [editor][camera] (the scene camera unchanged after orbiting; panning moves the view), [editor][prefab].

opportunities.title: Procedural generation kit, and saves that keep world edits
opportunities.evidence: sdk/runtime/pocket.ts:257-260: one random() stream seeded by the run, with no separate streams and no int, pick or shuffle helpers. Noise exists only inside the C++ terrain generator (engine/assets/src/terrain.cpp). The tilemap commands (session.cpp:5486) have no create or resize, so every map must start from a .tmj file. No command builds a mesh from vertex arrays. engine/app/src/session.cpp:3486-3496: a save slot holds the scene, script state and caller data only. tilemap.set and fill (dug tiles, generated dungeons), terrain.sculpt and paint (terraforming) and per-entity map copies are lost on load unless written over the project's own assets with tilemap.save or terrain.save.
opportunities.impact: Roguelikes and dungeon crawlers (fresh seeded floors, the same seed giving the same dungeon while combat randomness stays separate), sandbox and destructible-terrain games, voxel or procedural 3D levels, puzzle generators, and save and continue in all of them.
opportunities.plan: 1) SDK rng(seed): PCG32 matching engine/core's PCG32, with int, range, pick, shuffle and weighted; noise.perlin2/3, simplex2 and fbm on sdk/runtime/repro.ts math so lockstep stays exact. 2) tilemap.create {width, height, tile_size, tilesets, orientation} and tilemap.resize, building on the in-memory map documents the asset store already writes (docs/status.md:180). 3) mesh.create and mesh.update {name, positions, normals?, uvs?, colors?, indices}, sent as shared typed arrays the way world.pack works, registered as mem:<name> for MeshRenderer and for shape-3 Colliders (rebuild the physics mesh cache on update). 4) save.write includes changed map documents and terrain height and paint grids (beside the slot as files or base64), and save.read restores them before the scene. 5) A roguelike sample: a BSP dungeon on a created map, a nav rebake, save and load mid-floor; runtime_tests [saves][tilemap].

opportunities.title: Windows (then Linux) desktop builds
opportunities.evidence: pocket.toml:82 pins wgpu-native for macos-aarch64 only. engine/platform/src/platform.cpp:244 creates the native surface only through SDL_Metal_CreateView. docs/packaging.md:25: 'Windows and Linux packs arrive with those platforms (V8, ADR 0005)'. docs/status.md:212 and docs/decisions/0005-script-engine-backend.md: the V8 build recipe is unverified, and JavaScriptCore is the only native script backend. tools/pocket/src/toolchain.rs:84 looks only for Apple's Command Line Tools. ADR 0001:29 plans Windows (clang-cl) and Ubuntu CI.
opportunities.impact: The biggest reach gain available. It enables shipping to Steam, itch.io and stores on the platform most players use (Windows dominates PC gaming), which is the positioning's 'a desktop build for stores' job. Today the only outlets are unsigned Mac folders and the WebGPU web build.
opportunities.plan: 1) Script backend: link JavaScriptCore from a pinned prebuilt static build for windows-x64 and linux-x64 (for example Bun's WebKit releases), by sha256 like other prebuilts. It has the same C API, so engine/script/src/jsc_host.cpp stays as it is; V8 stays the long-term option behind ScriptHost. 2) Per-platform wgpu-native release zips in pocket.toml. 3) platform.cpp: build the surface from SDL3 window properties (Win32 HWND and HINSTANCE; X11 or Wayland display and surface) where macOS uses the Metal view. 4) toolchain.rs: LLVM clang-cl plus Windows SDK discovery (docs/build-system.md:78); foreign CMake builds for SDL3, FreeType and HarfBuzz. 5) pack.rs: an .exe folder or zip on Windows and a folder on Linux; CI on windows-2025 and ubuntu-24.04. 6) Proof: the arena lockstep game between Windows and macOS with equal hashes (the reproducible math already targets this).

opportunities.title: Scaling crowds and many units (RTS, hordes, tower defense)
opportunities.evidence: engine/nav/src/nav.cpp:837-858: each agent scans every other agent (O(n²)) and allocates its own std::vector<Near> every tick; the overlap push at nav.cpp:939-950 is O(n²) again. At 1000 agents that is about 1M distance tests in avoidance plus 0.5M in the push, and 1000 allocations, per tick. engine/renderer/src/animation.cpp:37-56 and 906-916: every animated entity builds per-tick Locals (5 vectors) plus std::map nodes and a path string, at least 8 heap allocations each, about double during cross-fades. engine/renderer/src/renderer.cpp:2480 caps joint matrices at kMaxJoints = 16384 per frame (about 250 rigs of 65 joints), and past that skinning is silently dropped (renderer.cpp:7735). engine/physics/src/physics.cpp:2372: every raycast visits every collider, and placed() (physics.cpp:20-27) allocates a parent-chain vector for every parented static body on every call. A Blender level makes all statics parented, and colliding particles cast one ray each per tick.
opportunities.impact: RTS, horde survival, tower defense, city and colony sims, and large 3D levels with many line-of-sight checks. These are the 'built to scale' claims of docs/positioning.md, measurable with the existing perf command and gpu_probe.
