summary:
Read-only study of /Users/qiulinfan/Desktop/aipocket, which is now on branch master; the task said agent-first. Nothing was built, run or modified. The data comes from 100 agent task runs in tests/evidence/agent-eval/*.json, plus the harness, the runner, the pi extension, the MCP server, command_help.cpp and session.cpp.

Where the money and turns go:
- The cost sits in script, mechanic and file tasks. These are double_jump, coin_respawn, jump_sound, lamp_prefab and walker_sprint (persian_locale and blender_level are in no full run).
- In each of the five full runs they took 51-85% of tokens, 45-70% of cost and 59-80% of time. coin_respawn alone took 24-58% of a run's tokens.
- In pi-deepseek-extension-2, the 7 script tasks made 98 file or shell calls against 36 engine calls. The 9 command tasks made 5 against 56.
- Across all 100 runs, total tokens grow as turns^1.62, wall time as turns^1.51 and DeepSeek cost as turns^1.1. Cutting turns on long tasks pays off more than linearly. Cache reads are 92-96% of every run's tokens.

The main structural cause is that the engine offers no way to apply an edit:
- project.reload only re-reads the bundle and the `.project.json` that `pocket ts` writes (session.cpp:4165-4207).
- Yet its help says scripts restart "after edits" (command_help.cpp:198). The stopped-simulation hints say "fix the script and project.reload" (session.cpp:5379, 5384, 5399), and following them reloads the old bundle.
- No MCP tool bundles a project, and the pi extension has none either. None of the 18 docs given to agents explains the bundle-then-reload loop.
- One run, omp-deepseek-mcp jump_sound, used the whole 600 s limit (600.2 s).

Other findings:
- **Silently ignored values.** Component values with unknown field names or wrong types are dropped without an error (gen.rs:282-290, 339), and world.set still answers {"ok": true}. For example `{Light: {kind: "point"}}` gives a directional light, because 9 enum-like fields are integer codes.
- **Cut-off command list.** The pi extension cuts results at 24,000 characters. `commands {usage:true}` is about 32.5 KB, so 46 of 204 commands are hidden, including project.reload/read/write, script.*, ui.*, water.height and scatter.copies. The cut note then suggests parameters that `commands` and `world.schema` do not accept.
- **Unused batching.** The control server already accepts JSON-RPC batches, but none of the agent-facing tools exposes them.
- **Missing and heavy docs.** The doc list is 337 KB (about 84k tokens). It leaves out input, audio, sprites, scenarios and environment, which the mechanic tasks need.
- **Unreliable call counts for oh-my-pi.** oh-my-pi routes MCP calls (per docs/mcp.md:27) through its `write` tool. Its extension runs record no `pocket` calls either, so its engine calls probably show up as `write` too, which can't be confirmed because no trace is kept. Either way its `write` counts mix engine calls with file writes.
- **No traces, no repeats.** The runner throws away the event stream. Each configuration ran once, while the same task varies about 2x between runs.

What the benchmark doesn't cover yet:
- debugging a broken game
- regression checks against the samples' own scenarios
- tuning feel to numbers
- framing or layout judged by eye
- bigger builds from scratch
- vague requests, since every task names its components and fields
- follow-up requests from the person directing the game
- cost as the project grows

Below are 13 changes ranked by value for effort, each with a concrete plan. The new benchmark tasks are the last two items on the benchmark itself.

opportunities.title: One call that applies an edit: bundle, type-check, reload and report (pocket apply / project_apply / pocket_apply), and fix the hints that point agents at a stale reload
opportunities.evidence:
- **What reload actually does.** project.reload re-reads only `options_.bundle` and the bundler's `<bundle>.project.json`. The comment at engine/app/src/session.cpp:4174 says "project.toml as the tool last bundled it"; the code is session.cpp:4165-4207, and the bundler writes that file at tools/pocket/src/commands.rs:398-433. The runtime cannot bundle by itself.
- **What agents are told.** project.reload's help says scripts restart "after edits" and project.toml is "read again" (engine/app/src/command_help.cpp:198). The hints on a stopped simulation say "fix the script and project.reload" (session.cpp:5379, 5384, 5399).
- **No tool for it.** No MCP tool bundles a project (tools/pocket/src/mcp.rs:39-138, 30 tools). The pi extension only has `pocket` and `pocket_look` (integrations/pi/pocket.ts:35-83). Of the 18 agent docs (tools/scripts/agent_eval.py:30), only localization.md mentions project.reload at all. The harness note says it will bundle "when you are done" (agent_eval.py:1062).
- **Measured effect.** In pi-deepseek-extension-2.json the 7 script tasks made 98 file/shell calls against 36 engine calls; the 9 command tasks made 5 against 56. The four design/file tasks were 85% of tokens and 70% of cost. In omp-deepseek-mcp-2 they were 82% of tokens. coin_respawn took 24-58% of a run's tokens in every full run.
- **One run hit the time cap.** omp-deepseek-mcp jump_sound used the whole 600 s limit (600.2 s, 21 calls; tools/scripts/runners/pi_agent.py:38 sets 600 s).
- **Settings edits are invisible too.** walker_sprint's project.toml edit has no effect on project.reload until the project is bundled again.
opportunities.impact: This is the biggest cost bucket: mechanic and file tasks are 51-85% of tokens in every full run. Tokens grow as turns^1.62 across the 100 runs. Cutting the 23-85 turns of coin_respawn or double_jump by a third should roughly halve their tokens and save about 40% of their wall time (time grows as turns^1.51). It would also let MCP-only agents, which have no shell, do script tasks at all.

opportunities.title: Instrument the benchmark: keep traces, sort calls by purpose, record errors, repeat runs
opportunities.evidence:
- **Only counts are kept.** tools/scripts/runners/pi_agent.py:124-147 keeps per-toolName counts, turns and usage, and drops the event stream: no arguments, no error texts, no per-turn tokens. tool_errors is a bare count (line 162).
- **oh-my-pi counts mix engine calls and file writes.** It routes MCP calls through its `write` tool on xd://mcp__pocket_* (docs/mcp.md:27). In command-only tasks where editing files is forbidden, its rows still show writes: night_lamp write 12-14, calm_lake write 17, stormy_dusk write 19. No oh-my-pi row records a single `pocket` call, even with --via extension.
- **One run per setup, 2x variance per task.** coin_respawn under oh-my-pi cost $0.047, $0.086 and $0.106 in three runs (377-568 s). Under pi it used 1.53M tokens in one run and 0.74M in another. reed_field passed one day and failed the next.
- **The writeup can't break down its own number.** agent-eval.md:82 says agents made "25 to 45 reads, greps and shell calls" in command tasks, with no breakdown of what they were.
opportunities.impact: This makes "where do the turns go" answerable from the evidence, and lets a 20-30% improvement or regression be told apart from noise. Every other item in this list needs it to be measured. It doesn't make agents cheaper by itself.

opportunities.title: Make the discovery commands fit and filter: commands, help and world.schema by family, search or component; compact output in the pi tool
opportunities.evidence:
- **The cut.** integrations/pi/pocket.ts:12 cuts any result at 24,000 characters (LIMIT) and pretty-prints JSON (line 31). `commands {usage: true}` comes to about 32.5 KB pretty-printed for 204 entries (engine/app/src/command_help.cpp). The cut falls after `terrain.info`, entry 157, and hides 46 commands: terrain.height, terrain.paint, terrain.sculpt, water.height, wind.at, scatter.copies, locale.*, save.*, script.* (including script.eval), project.reload, project.read, project.write and ui.*.
- **help is worse.** `help {}` is about 56 KB.
- **The way out doesn't exist.** The cut note says to "ask for less, e.g. a depth, a limit or one entity" (pocket.ts:32). But `commands` only takes `usage?` (command_help.cpp:20). `world.schema` takes nothing (command_help.cpp:40) and dumps all 40 components with docs and defaults (engine/world/src/world.cpp:602-624). Unknown keys are refused (session.cpp:5208-5216), so the agent can't narrow either one.
- **Over MCP the full list is never cut but stays in context.** `runtime_commands` returns the whole ~8k-token list, which is then re-read on every later turn.
opportunities.impact: Medium. pi with the extension was the cheapest setup measured (3.1M tokens for 16 tasks, against 8.2-10.2M for oh-my-pi over MCP on 15). This fixes what that setup can see, and cuts the context discovery leaves behind on every later turn.
opportunities.plan:
1. Add filters:
   - `commands {family?: 'terrain', search?: 'water', usage?}`;
   - `help {command? | family? | search?}`;
   - `world.schema {component? | components?: [...]}`, returning only that component's fields with name, type, default, doc and enum names.
   Update the param lists in command_help.cpp.
2. Make usage answers compact, one line each: `world.set {entity, component, value, cause?} — summary`, joined as text rather than pretty JSON. All 204 come to about 20 KB.
3. In pocket.ts, use compact JSON for array results and make the cut note specific to the command ("commands {family}", "world.schema {component}").
4. Add a runtime test that `commands {usage:true}` stays under the extension's LIMIT.

opportunities.title: Refuse unknown component fields and wrong types, accept enum names, and have world.set answer with the resulting value
opportunities.evidence:
- **Unknown keys and wrong types are dropped.** The generated from_json reads only the keys it knows (tools/pocket/src/gen.rs:282-290). scalar_from_json drops a value of the wrong type, so a string given for an i32 is ignored (gen.rs:339).
- **And still reported as success.** World::set merges and succeeds (engine/world/src/world.cpp:418-430), and world.set answers {"ok": true} (engine/app/src/session.cpp:4627-4632). So `{Light: {kind: "point"}}` makes a directional light, and typos such as `colour` vanish without a word.
- **Enums are integer codes explained in prose.** 9 fields work this way, in engine/world/meta/components.toml: Light.kind :99, RigidBody.kind :462, Joint.kind :478, Collider.shape :684, the camera rig's mode :76, Sky.mode :156 (3 = the atmosphere, which stormy_dusk needs), root_motion :377, NavAgent mode :736 and state :747.
- **The docs already show what this costs.** This is the field-level version of the parameter bug that cost "a dozen calls" before commands began refusing unknown keys (agent-eval.md:82, docs/mcp.md:37).
opportunities.impact: This closes the last silent-failure path in every spawn, set and instantiate an agent makes. Agents also stop reading docs to look up enum codes. Medium-high value for command tasks and for scripts written against the same records.
opportunities.plan:
1. Have gen.rs emit a list of known field names per component and record.
2. At the command boundary (world.set, world.spawn, world.instantiate components), check the value's keys recursively and its types. Fail with `bad_args`, for example: "MeshRenderer has no field 'colour'; did you mean 'color'? fields: …". Reuse the edit-distance suggestion (command_suggestions in command_help.cpp).
3. Keep scene and prefab loading lenient: log a warning instead of failing, so existing files keep working.
4. Add `enum = ["directional","point","spot"]` to the 9 fields in components.toml. The generator should accept a name or a number. world.schema shows the names; scenes keep storing numbers.
5. Make world.set answer {ok: true, value: <the component after the merge>}, so a set is checked in the same call.

opportunities.title: Lay out the docs for agents: one short guide and topic help built from the metadata, instead of 18 design docs
opportunities.impact: Medium-high. It cuts doc reads in command tasks and the design time in mechanic tasks, and it is a prerequisite for tasks outside the current doc list.

opportunities.title: Expose batched calls in the pi tool, MCP runtime_command and pocket rpc
opportunities.impact: Fewer turns for command tasks and for the observe-after-change pattern (set, then step, then read). Each saved turn saves a full re-read of the context: tokens grow as turns^1.62 and time as turns^1.51.
opportunities.plan:
1. Give the pi tool `calls?: [{method, params}]`. It POSTs an array and returns [{result} | {error, code}], keeping error.data.code, which today is dropped at pocket.ts:25.
2. Give MCP `runtime_command` the same `calls`.
3. Have `pocket rpc` accept a JSON array as its single argument.
4. On the server, add `stop_on_error` (on by default) so a batch stops at its first failure, with the answer marking the calls it skipped.
5. Say so in the tool descriptions and in docs/agents.md ("set, step and read in one call").

opportunities.title: A cheap first look at a project: project.brief
opportunities.evidence:
- **project.info says almost nothing.** It returns only the name, directories, bundle, font, contexts and window (engine/app/src/session.cpp:4152-4164).
- **Getting oriented takes several calls today:** world.tree, state, input.describe, assets.list, reading the scripts, reading docs.
- **What a first look costs now.** pi's first turns cost about 6-17k tokens; oh-my-pi's 13-20k. Command tasks with near-zero design still took 7-36 calls under oh-my-pi.
- **The samples are small.** Scripts are 59-209 lines and scenes 0.8-15 KB. Real games will be 10-100x bigger, and discovery cost grows with them.
- **What exists is a set of single views.** The perception tools (world.tree, transcript, world.lint) each show one thing; none summarises a project.
opportunities.impact: Medium now, larger as projects grow. It replaces the first 3-6 calls of most tasks with one call of about 1.5k tokens.

opportunities.title: Play and watch in one call: watch/until on step and env.step
opportunities.evidence:
- **Checking a jump by hand is hundreds of calls.** The harness's double_jump check makes up to about 320 step/state calls: 240 one-tick steps to land, then 80 to find the apex (tools/scripts/agent_eval.py:258-282).
- **Agents check their own mechanics the same way.** pi double_jump: 17 engine calls and 23 shell calls. omp-deepseek-mcp double_jump: 51 turns, 59 calls, 2.0M tokens.
- **The one-call version exists but falls short.** env.step already acts, steps and observes in one call (docs/design/environment.md; command_help.cpp:135). But it returns only the end state, and environment.md and scenarios.md are not in the agent docs.
opportunities.impact: Medium on mechanic and tuning tasks, which is where the cost is. Checking a jump becomes 2 calls instead of tens.
opportunities.plan:
1. Add parameters to `step` and `env.step`:
   - `watch: [keys]`, returning per key {min, max, tick_of_max, first, last, changes};
   - optional `every: n` for a sampled series;
   - `until: {key, op, value}`, which stops early, for example on landing.
   Fill them from state_history_, which transcript already uses.
2. Document them in docs/agents.md with the double-jump check as the example:
   - `env.step {actions:{jump:true}, ticks:12}`
   - `env.step {actions:{jump:true}, ticks:80, watch:['player.y']}`

opportunities.title: Benchmark: debugging a broken game, regression guards and tuning feel
opportunities.evidence:
- **What the 29 tasks cover** (docs/agent-eval.md:9-39):
  - none starts from a broken game;
  - events.why is needed only by event_cause;
  - world.lint, recorder.*, transcript, scenarios and analyze.* are never needed.
- **Nothing checks for collateral damage.** No task re-runs the sample's own scenarios after an edit, though 8 samples ship scenarios (samples/{arena,drive,hills,physics,playground,sprites,ui,walker}/scenarios).
- **The writeup says so itself.** "none is timed, and none needs art drawn, a level laid out or a scene composed by eye" (agent-eval.md:96). status.md Next #3 asks for more tasks.
- **The tools are already built.** The perception design (docs/design/agent-perception.md) exists for exactly this kind of debugging.
opportunities.impact: It measures the work agent-perception.md was built for: finding out why something broke, and getting a feel right. It also catches mechanic edits that break the rest of the game, which the current checks miss.
opportunities.plan:
Add tasks with mechanical checks to agent_eval.py:
1. `fall_through` (a walker copy): the harness breaks the floor, for example RigidBody kind 0, or Collider shape 3 with a missing mesh. The agent gets only the symptom: "the player falls through the floor". Check: walk.ts passes at 3 seeds, and only the floor changed.
2. `frozen_coin` (a sprites copy): inject a script error that fires on the second coin, for example a world.set on a destroyed id like the crash in the first MCP run. Symptom only. Check: coins.ts and bots.ts pass.
3. `floaty_jump`: "apex 3.0±0.1 above the ground, 0.9±0.05 s in the air". Check against the player.y and grounded series.
4. `slow_swarm` (swarm): "tick.ms under X" in the release runtime, read through `perf`.
5. A regression guard for every script task: after the check, run `pocket scenario <copy> --seeds 3` and report regressions in their own column.

opportunities.title: Benchmark: work judged by eye, bigger builds, vague requests and follow-ups
opportunities.evidence:
- **Tasks spell out the exact API.** For example night_lamp says "a Light of kind 1, color r 1, g 0.7, b 0.4, intensity 3, range 6" (tools/scripts/agent_eval.py:984). So the benchmark measures following a spec, not reading intent.
- **The projects are small samples:** scripts of 59-209 lines.
- **Each task is one-shot.** No task has a second message from the person directing.
- **Nothing is judged by eye.** No task asks for camera framing or level layout (agent-eval.md:96).
- **No task covers cameras, particles, timelines, joints or the editor,** though their docs are in the agent doc list or the engine.
opportunities.impact: This widens what the benchmark can claim, from "makes the right call" to "helps you make your game". That is the thesis, and the benchmark doesn't measure it yet.
opportunities.plan:
1. `frame_shot`: place the camera so the Ball is centred within 10% and covers 5-15% of the frame, with the Beacon visible. Check with render.visible coverage and centre.
2. `platform_climb`: lay out five platforms from the ground to a flag at y 8. Check that a scripted bot (run toward the next platform, jump at its edge) reaches the flag within 20 s at 3 seeds. Save render.views for a separate human or vision-model rubric, not part of pass/fail.
3. `coin_game_from_scratch`: `pocket new`, WASD movement, 5 coins, a score label and a "You win" label. Check with an env.step bot and ui.query, on a 15-minute budget.
4. Vague twins of 5 command tasks, for example "make the ball look like lacquered car paint", checked against ranges.
5. Two-message follow-up tasks ("too dark: warmer and twice as bright"), with the runner keeping the agent's session between messages.
6. A scaling pair: the same three tasks on hello and on showcase (or a synthetic project 10x the size), to measure how much more the first look costs.

opportunities.title: Rotation and aiming helpers: yaw/pitch/roll and look_at for Transform, commands and the SDK
opportunities.evidence:
- **Rotations exist only as quaternions.** Transform.rotation is parsed from x, y, z, w only (tools/pocket/src/gen.rs:338).
- **No helpers anywhere.** sdk/runtime has no euler or look-at helper; animation.ts LookAt only aims skeleton nodes. No command aims an entity.
- **The reference solution itself is heavy.** stormy_dusk's reference needs about 10 lines of quaternion math (agent_eval.py:919-934).
- **Agents pay for it.** In omp-deepseek-full, stormy_dusk took 25 turns, 36 calls (5 of them `eval` to compute rotations), 1.13M tokens and $0.020, the most expensive command task. The same agent's dedicated run took 13 turns.
- **Even the scaffold hard-codes them.** It writes camera quaternions by hand (commands.rs: rotation {x: -0.26, …, w: 0.97}).
opportunities.impact: Medium for lighting, cameras, composition and level layout: exactly the eye-judged work the benchmark doesn't measure yet.
opportunities.plan:
1. In world.set/spawn Transform values, also accept `rotation: {yaw, pitch, roll}` in degrees and `look: {x, y, z}` or `look_at: entity | point`. Turn them into a quaternion when set; scenes keep storing quaternions.
2. Add a command `world.look_at {entity, at | direction, up?}`.
3. Add SDK `quat.fromEuler` and `quat.lookAt`.
4. Add a line on sun elevation and azimuth to the Light docs and to docs/agents.md.

opportunities.title: Report effective world-space values so unit mistakes show up in observations
opportunities.evidence:
- **The reed_field failure was a unit mistake.** It failed in omp-deepseek-full because Scatter.collide is in the entity's units (engine/world/meta/components.toml:638): the agent's 0.1 on an entity scaled 0.1 came out as 0.01 (agent-eval.md:91; the row's detail says the radius is 0.010).
- **The engine never reports the real number.** The check has to compute collide × scale × size itself (agent_eval.py:905-913). scatter.copies returns only point, size and shade.
- **The same trap recurs:**
  - Collider sizes are half extents (blender_level's task text has to say so);
  - the raft's default mass sinks it, so the agent had to infer buoyancy from docs (agent-eval.md:86).
opportunities.impact: Medium. It turns a class of failures that only a hidden check catches into one the agent sees in its own reading of the world, at no extra calls.
opportunities.plan:
1. Have scatter.copies return `collider: {radius, height}` in world units.
2. Add `world.describe {entity, effective: true}`, which also reports world-space collider extents, a light's range in world units, and a body's mass, density and buoyancy against the water under it.
3. Add world.lint warnings for a body denser than the water it is in, and for a collider smaller than 1 cm.

opportunities.title: A game-making profile for the MCP server with instructions on the loop
opportunities.evidence:
- **The tool list is large and mostly for engine developers.** tools_list has 30 tools, about 11.5 KB of schema (tools/pocket/src/mcp.rs:39-138), sent with every request. It includes pocket_build, pocket_test, pocket_gen and pocket_doctor.
- **The instructions start with building.** initialize says "Build with pocket_build, test with pocket_test…" (mcp.rs:392), and runtime_start always builds the debug runtime (mcp.rs:180).
- **Smaller setups were cheaper, but the comparison is muddied by the agent.**
  - pi with 2 tools: $0.15 and 3.1M tokens for 16 tasks.
  - oh-my-pi over MCP: $0.22-0.30 and 8.2-10.2M tokens for 15 tasks.
  - oh-my-pi from the repo root: 27 min; from outside it: 12.6 min.
opportunities.impact: Medium, but the evidence mixes agent and interface differences, so measure it with the instrumentation item. It also keeps game-making agents from rebuilding the engine.
